KP18 The Probabilistic Neural Network (PNN)

Level: undergraduate, year 3

Pattern Recognition | Chapter 4, §4.17

Slides: read and download

Learning objectives

  • Explain how a PNN moves the Parzen estimate into a network and how unit-norm normalization turns a distance into an inner product.
  • Write the hidden and output layers of a PNN and compute the outputs and the class on a small example.
  • Explain the cost and the limit of a PNN: a hidden layer as large as the training set and a normalization that discards the length.

KP18 The Probabilistic Neural Network (PNN)

One-sentence summary: A Parzen estimate is an average of kernels, so give every training point one neuron; after normalizing the vectors to length 1 the squared distance becomes an inner product and the formula takes the form of a network. Training is copying the data, and the price is keeping every training point.

1. One neuron per point

Plain explanation: Is there a network that needs almost no training?

  • Parzen estimate: a kernel (Gaussian here) on every training point, averaged to estimate the class density p^(x∣ω)\hat p(x\mid\omega)p^​(x∣ω).
  • Kernel width hhh: the width of the kernel; larger is smoother and smaller hugs the individual training points.

The Bayes decision compares the largest P(ωi) p^(x∣ωi)P(\omega_i)\,\hat p(x\mid\omega_i)P(ωi​)p^​(x∣ωi​). A sum of kernels is easy to compute in parallel, so every training point gets one neuron.

Figure lec05-kp18-parzen: five one-dimensional training points with a kernel each, averaged into the estimated density.

2. Distance becomes inner product

Unit-norm normalization: divide every feature vector by its own length ∥x∥=∑jxj2\|x\|=\sqrt{\sum_jx_j^2}∥x∥=∑j​xj2​​ so that its length becomes 1. Expanding the squared distance

∥x−xi∥2=∥x∥2+∥xi∥2−2xiTx, \|x-x_i\|^2=\|x\|^2+\|x_i\|^2-2x_i^Tx, ∥x−xi​∥2=∥x∥2+∥xi​∥2−2xiT​x,

it equals 2−2xiTx2-2x_i^Tx2−2xiT​x when both lengths are 1. Example: x=(0.6,0.8)x=(0.6,0.8)x=(0.6,0.8), xi=(1,0)x_i=(1,0)xi​=(1,0): inner product 0.60.60.6 and squared distance 2−1.2=0.82-1.2=0.82−1.2=0.8; directly (0.4)2+0.82=0.8(0.4)^2+0.8^2=0.8(0.4)2+0.82=0.8, the same.

Figure lec05-kp18-circle: two vectors on the unit circle and the chord between them.

3. The discriminant

Formal definition: after substituting ∥x−xi∥2=2−2xiTx\|x-x_i\|^2=2-2x_i^Tx∥x−xi​∥2=2−2xiT​x and dropping the common 1/((2π)l/2hl)1/((2\pi)^{l/2}h^l)1/((2π)l/2hl),

g(ωm)=P(ωm)Nm∑i=1Nmexp⁡(xiTx−1h2). g(\omega_m)=\frac{P(\omega_m)}{N_m}\sum_{i=1}^{N_m}\exp\Bigl(\frac{x_i^Tx-1}{h^2}\Bigr). g(ωm​)=Nm​P(ωm​)​i=1∑Nm​​exp(h2xiT​x−1​).

Check (h=0.8h=0.8h=0.8): for the unit vector x=(0.6,0.8)x=(0.6,0.8)x=(0.6,0.8) the distance form exp⁡(−∥x−xi∥2/2h2)\exp(-\|x-x_i\|^2/2h^2)exp(−∥x−xi​∥2/2h2) and the inner-product form exp⁡((xiTx−1)/h2)\exp((x_i^Tx-1)/h^2)exp((xiT​x−1)/h2) both give 0.53530.53530.5353. Common misconception: the formula can be used without normalizing. For x=(1.2,1.6)x=(1.2,1.6)x=(1.2,1.6), not a unit vector, the distance form gives 0.13120.13120.1312 and the inner-product form 1.36681.36681.3668, far apart; normalization is required.

Figure lec05-kp18-kernels: the two forms for a unit and a non-unit vector.

4. The architecture

Probabilistic neural network (PNN): the formula above moved into a network. The input layer has lll nodes; the hidden layer has NNN nodes, the weights of node kkk are the kkk-th training vector and its output is yk=exp⁡((xkTx−1)/h2)y_k=\exp((x_k^Tx-1)/h^2)yk​=exp((xkT​x−1)/h2); the output layer has one linear combiner per class connected only to the hidden nodes of that class: outputm=P(ωm)Nm∑yk\text{output}_m=\tfrac{P(\omega_m)}{N_m}\sum y_koutputm​=Nm​P(ωm​)​∑yk​, and the largest wins. This network needs almost no training: no gradient descent, no local minima, no epochs.

Figure lec05-kp18-arch: two inputs, five hidden nodes and two outputs.

Example (designed here): class A at 20°,40°,60°20°,40°,60°20°,40°,60°, class B at 100°,120°100°,120°100°,120°, test vector at 70°70°70°, h=0.5h=0.5h=0.5, priors 0.5. Hidden outputs yky_kyk​: A: 0.2396,0.5851,0.94100.2396,0.5851,0.94100.2396,0.5851,0.9410; B: 0.5851,0.23960.5851,0.23960.5851,0.2396. Outputs: A =0.53×1.7658=0.2943=\tfrac{0.5}{3}\times1.7658=0.2943=30.5​×1.7658=0.2943; B =0.52×0.8247=0.2062=\tfrac{0.5}{2}\times0.8247=0.2062=20.5​×0.8247=0.2062; A wins.

Figure lec05-kp18-toy: the five hidden outputs and the two class outputs.

6. The kernel width

Example (designed here): two classes distinguished by direction (means 40°40°40° and 110°110°110°, sd 25°25°25°) with random lengths; 50 training and 500 new points per class, normalized and fed to a PNN. h=0.02h=0.02h=0.02 gives 95% on training (the classes overlap, so never 100%) and 89.6% on new points (hugging single points); h=0.1∼1h=0.1\sim1h=0.1∼1 gives about 91.6%; h=5h=5h=5 still gives 91.0%. A single cut at 75°75°75° gets 91.9% on new points and the PNN is close to it; this easy example is insensitive to hhh and only a very small hhh hurts.

Figure lec05-kp18-hcurve: accuracy against the kernel width hhh.

7. How many points

The same data with nnn training points per class, h=0.3h=0.3h=0.3, 20 random draws each. Mean accuracy on new points: n=2n=2n=2: 88.3% (sd 0.07); n=10n=10n=10: 91.8% (0.011); n=50n=50n=50: 92.0%; n=200n=200n=200: 92.0%. This easy data need not be kept in full; fewer points mean a smaller network.

Figure lec05-kp18-nsub: training points per class against accuracy on new points.

8. The cost

Each test point needs N⋅lN\cdot lN⋅l multiply-adds and N⋅lN\cdot lN⋅l stored numbers (8 bytes each): N=100,l=2N=100,l=2N=100,l=2: 200 operations, 1.6 KB; N=104,l=10N=10^4,l=10N=104,l=10: 10510^5105 operations, 0.8 MB; N=106,l=100N=10^6,l=100N=106,l=100: 10810^8108 operations, 0.8 GB. To remember: PNN = a parallel hardware version of the Parzen estimate; training is copying data and inference computes everything, moving the learning cost to the inference cost. It sits at one end of a spectrum with sparsification (KP21): keep all against keep only the support vectors (source).

Figure lec05-kp18-cost: the cost table for work and memory.

Extension: the price of normalization, practice and worked solution

The price of normalization (designed here): concentric rings whose classes differ only in radius (about 1.0 against 2.2), 200 points each, half for training and half for testing. After normalization both classes sit on the unit circle with the same angle distribution and the PNN gets only 49.5% on new points, which is guessing. Normalization discards the length; before using a PNN check that the class information lies in the direction and not in the length.

Figure lec05-kp18-rings: left two concentric rings, right after normalization.
